function: Learned joint sub-band allocation and discrete transmit-power control of UAV-to-UAV links, reusing U2I spectrum, to minimize transmission delay under jamming and co-channel interference. p. 7
system: 10-30 UAVs at 100 m, U2U and U2I links to a ground BS; OFDM, 1.5 MHz sub-bands; Rician fading; antennas and carrier frequency not stated. p. 4, 10-11
method: Embodied multi-agent double DQN with prioritized experience replay and experience-transfer learning; reinforcement learning, shared replay buffer, decentralized execution; RMSProp, lr 0.008. p. 8-10
data_channel: Simulated urban macrocell (3GPP TR 36.777 assumptions, log-normal shadowing, Rician fading); Section V testbed with USRP N210 and Raspberry Pi measures channel gains. p. 4-5, 10, 13
test_conditions: Agents train in simulation, then testing rounds sweep UAV number (10-30), sub-bands (7-19) and jammer power (21-25 dBm); retraining per setting is not stated. p. 11-13
baselines: Learned only: DQN-based and DDQN-based approaches (text, p. 11); figure legends show E-MA-DDQN-IRA, E-MA-Dueling-DDQN-PER-TL-IRA, DDQN-PER-TL-IRA. No non-learned baseline. p. 11-12
metrics: Average total U2U delay and average U2I delay per link (s), probability of successful transmission, training reward. p. 11, 13
complexity: Order of complexity given: O(A*T*S0*sum of layer-size products) for MA-DDQN, O(Ba log2 D) for PER; TL compresses iterations to iota*T; no runtime or FLOPs. p. 10
q1_support: p. 13: "The channel gains of from all UAV to any receiver are measured in this experiment setting." Section V compares the agents on channel gains measured with a USRP N210 receiver and Raspberry Pi UAV nodes; Section IV uses a custom Rician/log-normal model (p. 4), so the mark rests on the measured data.
q2_support: p. 11: "the ET type is chosen because it can leverage the experiences obtained during the learning phases of other algorithms, i.e., DDQN and Q-learning". The transfer source is other algorithms in the same environment; Figs. 4-10 sweep UAV number, sub-bands and jamming power without stating that agents trained under other settings are reused; not met.
q3_support: p. 11: "benchmarked against two alternative approaches: the method based on DQN and the method based on DDQN". Both are learned; the figure legends (pp. 12-13) add only DRL variants and no non-learned method (random, greedy, optimization) is compared, so the classical comparison is missing; not met.
q4_support: p. 10: "the computational complexity is analyzed based on the number of agents". Section III-C gives the order of complexity of MA-DDQN, O(Ba log2 D) for PER, and the TL iteration compression; no runtime or operation count.
q5_support: p. 13: "The ground receiver was implemented using a USRP N210 to measure the received signal strength." The agents are trained and compared on measured channel gains (Section V); no code or data link is given, so the mark rests on the measured-data clause only.
notes: Title and DOI on page 1 match the file. Included in area 6: the learned DDQN agents choose transmit power and sub-band of UAV-to-UAV links (p. 7, Eq. 19), which is resource and power control of aerial links; the paper frames the goal as anti-jamming, an excluded function when alone, but the learned decisions are area 6. UAV trajectory is planned by simulated annealing, not learned (p. 4, p. 10). Flags for the reviewer: (1) q1 and q5 rest on the measured channel gains of Section V (p. 13); the simulation (p. 10) cites 3GPP TR 36.777 assumptions and its path loss (Eqs. 5-6), another standardized model, but its shadowing and Rician fading are custom, and there is no code or data link. (2) q2 is 0 because no new scenario is stated, although the conclusion (p. 14) claims transfer across deployment scenarios. (3) Text (p. 11) names DQN and DDQN baselines but the figure legends show other DRL variants; no non-learned baseline in either.
